title: Provable Training Data Identification for Large Language Models
claim: Our method keeps the realized error rate at or below the target level across scores while achieving substantial detection power.
layout: 2×3 grid of dual-axis bar/line plots; rows by dataset, columns by model
description: A 2-row by 3-column grid of dual-axis charts. Rows are datasets, (a) WikiMIA and (b) ArXivTection. Columns are models: NeoX-20B, LLaMA-7B and Pythia-6.9B. Each subplot has the target false identification rate alpha (0.1 to 0.5) on the x-axis. Solid lines with markers show the realized FIR on the left axis, and a dashed gray diagonal marks the target. Bars show power on the right axis. Four detection scores are color-coded: Perplexity in blue, Zlib in purple, MIN-K% in orange and M-Entropy in magenta. All four FIR lines cluster just below the diagonal, showing control of the error rate. Bars grow with alpha, and MIN-K% is usually the tallest. Power is higher on ArXivTection than on WikiMIA. The eye goes first to the bright bars, then to the lines hugging the diagonal.
caption: \metricabbr{} (solid lines) and Power (bars) achieved by our method when applied to various detection scores across a range of levels $\alpha$ (target \metricabbr{}). Each subplot corresponds to a specific model–dataset pair, and the dashed diagonal line indicates the target $\alpha$.
abstract: Identifying training data of large-scale models is critical for copyright litigation, privacy auditing, and ensuring fair evaluation. However, existing works typically treat this task as an instance-wise identification without controlling the error rate of the identified set, which cannot provide statistically reliable evidence. In this work, we formalize training data identification as a set-level inference problem and propose Provable Training Data Identification (PTDI), a distribution-free approach that enables provable and strict false identification rate control. Specifically, our method computes conformal p-values for each data point using a set of known unseen data and then develops a novel Jackknife-corrected Beta boundary (JKBB) estimator to estimate the training-data proportion of the test set, which allows us to scale these p-values. By applying the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure to the scaled p-values, we select a subset of data points with provable and strict false identification control. Extensive experiments across various models and datasets demonstrate that PTDI achieves higher power than prior methods while strictly controlling the FIR.
